# Arthropod-borne viruses

> *A person in Singapore can catch dengue from a mosquito that bred in the water of a flower-pot
> plate a few doors away and bit in the middle of the day. An arbovirus spreads where its vector lives
> and bites, so the habits of a mosquito predict who is infected, where and when, and how infection is
> prevented.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why the spread of an arbovirus follows its vector, and relate the habits of *Aedes*
  mosquitoes to the control of dengue in Singapore.
- Sort the main arboviruses by vector and animal host, and predict from these where each one is
  caught and how infection is prevented.
- Explain why severe dengue is more likely in a second infection with a different serotype, and why
  its dangerous phase comes as the fever settles.
- Explain how Zika virus harms a fetus, and how it can reach a pregnant woman who has not been
  bitten.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main virus cause disease.
- Tell dengue virus from chikungunya virus by serotypes, the illness each causes and the main danger
  of each.
:::

## The group {#sec-arbo-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-arbo-sentence}

**Arboviruses** (arthropod-borne viruses) are viruses carried between vertebrate hosts by
blood-feeding arthropods, such as mosquitoes or ticks, in which they multiply, so where and when they
spread follows the arthropod. Dengue, Zika, chikungunya and Japanese encephalitis viruses are all
enveloped, with a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome. Most of the six questions have one
answer for the whole group; its members differ mainly in the arthropod and animal hosts that keep
each cycle going, and in the organ each one damages.

| Question | Answer for the arboviruses |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | Most have an RNA genome in a protein capsid, inside an envelope whose proteins bind host cells; in dengue, Zika, chikungunya and Japanese encephalitis viruses the RNA is single-stranded and positive-sense |
| How does it get energy? | It has no energy supply of its own and uses the host cell's, in the arthropod and in the vertebrate host |
| How does it copy itself and change? | A viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase copies the genome without proofreading, so variants arise readily; a positive-sense genome is translated by host ribosomes as soon as it is uncoated |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | In a cycle between a blood-feeding arthropod and vertebrate hosts, humans among them; spread by the bite of the arthropod, and not by touch or respiratory particles |
| How does damage happen? | Death of infected cells and the host's response to the infection, in the organs the virus reaches in the blood: leaking blood vessels in dengue, the fetal brain in Zika, the joints in chikungunya, the brain in Japanese encephalitis |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and other viral enzymes, although no drug against them is in routine use, so prevention rests on controlling the mosquitoes or ticks and on vaccines |

The genome of a positive-sense RNA virus is itself an mRNA, and the virus must supply its own
RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to copy it (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)). That polymerase does not proofread,
so copying errors stay in the new genomes (see [*How viruses
change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-mutation)). The name *arbovirus* describes a route of spread,
and the arboviruses come from several virus families, some with other kinds of RNA genome (see [*A
map of the viruses*](virus-map.qmd#sec-vmap-names)). Dengue virus, Zika virus and Japanese
encephalitis virus are flaviviruses; chikungunya virus is an alphavirus, from a different family.
The flaviviruses are similar enough that antibodies raised against one bind the others, so an
antibody test for one flavivirus can be positive after infection with another (see [*Detecting and
controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-serology)). In the first days of
illness, while the virus is in the blood, a **nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)**, a test that
copies a target sequence many times until it can be detected, finds its RNA and so identifies the
virus directly (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-methods)).

Each of these viruses depends on its **vector**, an arthropod that carries an organism between hosts
(see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-routes)). Mosquitoes are **biological
vectors** of these viruses: vectors in which the organism develops or multiplies, and which cannot
pass it on until it has done so (the same terms are used for parasites in [*Life cycles and
vectors*](../parasites/life-cycles.qmd#sec-life-vectors), later in the book). Only female mosquitoes
bite, because they need blood to make their eggs. One cycle of transmission runs through five steps:

::: {.flow}
1. A female mosquito bites a person or animal with virus in the blood
2. The virus multiplies in the mosquito's gut and spreads to its salivary glands
3. Days later, the mosquito injects virus with its saliva at every bite
4. The virus multiplies in the skin and lymph nodes of the new host and enters the blood
5. Another mosquito takes up the virus from the blood
:::

The mosquito stays infected for the rest of its life. A person is a source of virus for mosquitoes
only during **viraemia**, the presence of virus in the blood (see [*Viruses and the
host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-spread)), which lasts for several days around the start of the fever.
Virus in the blood can also pass to another person without a mosquito, though rarely: in transfused
blood or a transplanted organ, and from a mother with viraemia to her baby around the time of birth,
which for chikungunya virus can cause severe illness in the baby. These are acute infections: the
immune response clears the virus from the blood within days (see [*Viruses and the
host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-acute)).

Spread by a biological vector has four consequences:

- The virus spreads only where its vector can live and breed, and faster in warm, wet weather, which
  lets mosquitoes multiply and shortens the time the virus takes to reach their saliva
- People do not pass these viruses to each other by touch or in respiratory particles, so a patient
  is a risk to others mainly through the mosquitoes that bite during the fever
- A traveller with viraemia can start local transmission in any place where the vector lives
- Removing the vector, or stopping it from biting, interrupts every infection it carries

Changes in climate and land use therefore alter where these viruses spread (see [*Transmission,
outbreaks and One Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-onehealth)).

Dengue and Zika viruses are carried mainly by *Aedes aegypti*, which lives in and around homes, and
also by *Aedes albopictus*; chikungunya virus is carried well by both. Both mosquitoes live in
Singapore, and their habits explain where these infections are caught:

- They bite by day, with peaks in the early morning and the late afternoon
- They lay their eggs in small collections of clean, still water, such as flower-pot plates, pails,
  blocked roof gutters and discarded containers
- Their eggs stick to the inner wall of a container just above the water, survive drying for months,
  and hatch when the container fills again

Control in Singapore therefore rests on removing breeding sites around homes: emptying, covering or
discarding containers that hold water, and clearing roof gutters. Singapore also releases male *Aedes
aegypti* carrying the bacterium *Wolbachia*. Male mosquitoes do not bite, and when they mate with wild
females the eggs do not hatch, so the number of *Aedes aegypti* falls (see [*The microbial
world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-harmless)).

No antiviral drug is in routine use against any of these viruses. Treatment supports the patient
while the immune response clears the infection, and prevention rests on control of the vector,
protection from bites and, for some of these viruses, vaccines (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)).

### Sorting the group {#sec-arbo-key}

Arboviruses are named for a route of spread, so we sort them by the vector that carries them and the
vertebrate hosts that keep each cycle going. Some arboviruses are carried by ticks; those that matter
most in Singapore and South-East Asia are carried by mosquitoes.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the arboviruses by vector and host]{.tree-title}

- Carried from person to person by *Aedes* mosquitoes, which breed near homes and bite by day
  - Leaking blood vessels and shock, more often in a second infection: dengue virus
  - Damage to the brain of a fetus, after infection in pregnancy: Zika virus
  - Severe joint pain that can last for months: chikungunya virus
- Carried from pigs and wading birds by *Culex* mosquitoes that breed in rice fields and bite at
  night
  - Inflammation of the brain in a few of those infected, most of them children: Japanese
    encephalitis virus
:::

The vector and its hosts predict where and when the virus is caught, and how infection is prevented:

| Vector and hosts | Where and when it is caught | Who is infected | How infection is prevented |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Aedes* mosquitoes, carrying the virus from person to person | In and around homes, in towns and cities of the tropics, including Singapore, during the day | Anyone without immunity who lives in or visits these places | Removing breeding sites near homes; protection from bites by day; releases of male *Aedes aegypti* carrying *Wolbachia* |
| The *Culex* mosquitoes that carry Japanese encephalitis virus from pigs and wading birds | In rural areas with rice fields and pigs, in the evening and at night | Children in rural areas where the virus is common, and travellers who spend long periods there | Vaccination; protection from bites at night |

Work through the key from the vector, and read at each branch what the trait predicts about the
virus.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/arbo-key.yml"></div>

## Main viruses {#sec-arbo-main}

### Dengue virus: four serotypes and leaking blood vessels {#sec-arbo-dengue}

Dengue virus is a flavivirus carried between people by *Aedes* mosquitoes, and it causes more human
infections than any other arbovirus. Dengue is **endemic** in Singapore, constantly present in the
population at a baseline level, with periodic large outbreaks (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-levels)). Most cases in Singapore are in
adults: decades of control of *Aedes* mosquitoes have reduced transmission, so many people reach
adulthood without having been infected.

The virus exists as four **serotypes**, variants of the virus distinguished by their surface
antigens, numbered dengue virus 1 to 4. Infection with one serotype gives lasting immunity to that
serotype, but protection against the other three is short-lived, so a person can have dengue more than
once. Large outbreaks in Singapore have followed a change in the serotype that predominates, because
few people are immune to the newly dominant one.

Four to ten days after the bite, the infection causes anything from no symptoms to a severe illness,
and most infections are silent or mild. The typical illness begins suddenly, with high fever, severe
headache, pain behind the eyes, aching muscles and joints, and often a rash. A low white cell count
and **thrombocytopenia**, a low platelet count, are common.

The dangerous phase comes as the fever settles, usually between the third and the seventh day of
illness, when the patient may seem to be recovering. In some patients, small blood vessels throughout
the body become leaky for a day or two. **Plasma leakage**, the escape of plasma from small blood
vessels into the tissues and body cavities, concentrates the blood, so the proportion of red cells in
it (the haematocrit) rises, and fluid collects around the lungs and in the abdomen. If enough plasma
is lost, the volume of blood falls until the circulation can no longer supply the organs, which is
shock. **Severe dengue** is dengue with shock or breathing difficulty from plasma leakage, severe
bleeding, or severe damage to an organ. The leak is caused largely by the host's response to the
infection, and the vessel walls are not destroyed: they recover after a day or two (see [*Microbes and
their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)).

Severe dengue is more likely in a second infection, with a serotype different from the first, than in
a first infection. Antibodies usually protect by binding a virus and blocking its attachment to cells
(see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-immune)). Once the short-lived
cross-protection has faded, antibodies left by an infection with one serotype bind a different
serotype without neutralising it, that is, without stopping it from infecting cells. White blood
cells that carry receptors for antibodies, such as monocytes and macrophages, then take up the
antibody-coated virus, so more cells are infected and more virus is made. This **antibody-dependent
enhancement**, increased infection of cells when antibodies bind a virus without neutralising it, is
thought to explain much of the extra risk of a second infection.

::: {.example}
A dengue vaccine must protect against all four serotypes at once. The first licensed dengue vaccine
increased the risk of severe dengue in vaccinated people who had never been infected, for whom
vaccination is thought to have acted like a first infection, and it was then recommended only for
people who had already had dengue. A newer dengue vaccine has since been licensed in several
countries.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Does one bout of dengue give immunity to dengue?
Some infections, such as measles, are caught only once, and people who have had dengue often assume
that they cannot catch it again. Recovery gives lasting immunity only to the serotype that caused the
illness. Protection against the other three serotypes is short-lived, so a person can have dengue up
to four times, and a second infection with a different serotype carries a greater risk of severe
dengue than the first. A past infection is therefore a reason for more care with mosquito bites.
:::

In the first days of fever, the laboratory looks for the virus itself, as its RNA by NAAT or as a
viral protein by an antigen test; antibodies appear later and are more useful after the first few days
(see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-methods)). No
antiviral drug is in routine use against dengue virus. Treatment rests on close monitoring through
the days when the fever settles, and on careful replacement of fluid matched to the leak: too little
leaves the patient in shock, and too much overloads the circulation when the leak stops and the fluid
returns to the vessels. Anti-inflammatory drugs that impair platelet function are avoided, because
they increase the risk of bleeding.

Dengue virus harms the person infected in three ways:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Fever and aching | The virus multiplies in white blood cells and spreads in the blood; the host's response to the infection causes fever and aching | Sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes and aching muscles and joints in a young adult in Singapore |
| Plasma leakage and shock | As the fever settles, small blood vessels leak plasma for a day or two; the blood becomes concentrated and its volume falls | Restlessness, cold hands and falling blood pressure on the fifth day of illness, a day after the fever has gone |
| Bleeding | Thrombocytopenia, platelets that work poorly, fragile small vessels and disturbed clotting; severe bleeding often follows prolonged shock | Small red spots in the skin and bleeding from the gums; in severe dengue, bleeding from the gut |

Three conditions let dengue virus cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Anyone without immunity to the infecting serotype; severe dengue is more likely in a second infection with a different serotype | Immunity is specific to each serotype, and antibodies from an earlier infection with another serotype can increase the number of cells infected |
| Where (setting) | Towns and cities of the tropics where *Aedes* mosquitoes breed near homes, including Singapore, where dengue is endemic | The mosquitoes breed in small containers of clean water around homes and bite by day |
| How (route) | The bite of an infected female *Aedes* mosquito | The virus multiplies in the skin and lymph nodes, then spreads in the blood, from which the next mosquito takes it up |

Step through the two routes of dengue virus: from a bite to the next mosquito, and a second infection
that leads to severe dengue.

### Zika virus: harm to the fetus {#sec-arbo-zika}

Zika virus is a flavivirus, related to dengue virus and carried by the same *Aedes* mosquitoes. Most
infections cause no symptoms; the rest cause a mild illness lasting a few days, with an itchy rash,
red eyes, aching joints and little or no fever. Rarely, the infection is followed by
**Guillain–Barré syndrome**, a paralysis that develops over days to weeks as the immune response
damages the peripheral nerves.

**Microcephaly** is an abnormally small head, usually because the brain has not grown normally. During
a large epidemic in Brazil in 2015, a rise in the number of babies born with microcephaly showed that
Zika virus can harm the fetus. When a woman is infected during pregnancy, the virus can cross the
placenta and infect the dividing cells that form the nerve cells of the fetal brain. These cells die
or stop dividing, so the brain fails to develop, and the eyes can be damaged too. This is
**congenital infection**, infection passed from mother to fetus before birth, and it can follow an
infection that caused the mother no symptoms. Not every infected pregnancy is affected, and the risk
to the fetus is greatest when infection comes early in pregnancy.

Zika virus also spreads by sexual contact, which sets it apart from dengue and chikungunya viruses.
It persists in semen for weeks, and sometimes months, after it has cleared from the blood, so a
pregnant woman can be infected by a partner returning from an area with Zika without being bitten
herself. Protection in pregnancy therefore combines avoiding mosquito bites and areas with outbreaks
with protection during sex. Singapore had a local outbreak of Zika in 2016, spread by local *Aedes* mosquitoes.

Zika virus does its harm mainly before birth:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Mild illness | The virus spreads in the blood, and the host's response causes rash, red eyes and aching joints | A few days of an itchy rash and red eyes, with little fever, in an adult during an outbreak |
| Damage to the fetal brain | The virus crosses the placenta and infects the dividing cells that form the nerve cells of the fetal brain, which die or stop dividing | Microcephaly in the baby of a woman who had a mild rash, or no symptoms, during pregnancy |

Three conditions let Zika virus cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A fetus whose mother is infected during pregnancy; anyone not previously infected can be infected | The developing brain is built by dividing cells that the virus infects; in adults the illness is usually mild, and only rarely followed by Guillain–Barré syndrome |
| Where (setting) | Places where *Aedes* mosquitoes live, during an outbreak; sex with an infected partner | Mosquitoes carry the virus from person to person, and the virus persists in semen for weeks, and sometimes months |
| How (route) | The bite of an infected *Aedes* mosquito, or sexual contact; then across the placenta | Virus in the mother's blood crosses the placenta to the fetus |

Step through the two routes by which Zika virus reaches beyond the person bitten: to the fetus, and
to a sexual partner.

<div data-island="body-map" data-src="/diagrams/route-zika.yml"></div>

### Chikungunya virus: fever and lasting joint pain {#sec-arbo-chikungunya}

Chikungunya virus is an alphavirus, from a different family from dengue and Zika viruses, but it is
carried by the same mosquitoes, *Aedes aegypti* and *Aedes albopictus*. It has caused outbreaks
across the tropics, including in Singapore. The name means 'that which bends up', after the stooped
posture of people with severe joint pain.

Unlike dengue and Zika viruses, chikungunya virus makes most of the people it infects ill. The virus
multiplies to high levels in the blood and infects the tissues of the joints, muscles and tendons, and
the inflammation it provokes causes a sudden high fever with severe pain in many joints, often the
hands, wrists and ankles on both sides of the body. The pain can be disabling, and a rash is common.
The fever settles within about a week, but in some patients pain and stiffness in the joints continue
for months after the virus has left the blood, more often in older adults. Bleeding and shock are
uncommon, and death is rare. The virus exists as a single serotype, and recovery is thought to give
lasting immunity. Vaccines against chikungunya virus have recently been licensed in some countries,
chiefly for travellers; prevention still rests mainly on control of the mosquitoes.

Chikungunya virus does its harm in the joints, during the illness and after it:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Fever and joint pain | The virus reaches high levels in the blood and infects the tissues of the joints and muscles, and the inflammation it provokes causes pain | Sudden high fever with pain in the fingers, wrists and ankles so severe that the patient cannot grip or walk |
| Joint pain that persists | Inflammation continues in the joints after the fever has settled and the virus has left the blood | Pain and stiffness in both wrists three months after the fever, in a 60-year-old |

Three conditions let chikungunya virus cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Anyone not previously infected; older adults are the most likely to have pain that lasts | Without an earlier infection a person has no immunity; the virus has a single serotype, so one infection is thought to give lasting protection |
| Where (setting) | Places where *Aedes* mosquitoes live, during an outbreak | Both *Aedes aegypti* and *Aedes albopictus* carry the virus between people |
| How (route) | The bite of an infected *Aedes* mosquito | The virus spreads in the blood to the joints and infects their tissues |

Step through the route chikungunya virus takes, from a mosquito bite to the joints.

## Contrast pair {#sec-arbo-pairs}

### Dengue virus and chikungunya virus {#sec-arbo-pair-dengue-chikungunya}

Dengue and chikungunya viruses are carried by the same mosquitoes and circulate in the same places,
and both begin with sudden fever, rash and joint pain. Compare them feature by feature before reading
the principle.

## Beyond the main viruses {#sec-arbo-beyond}

### Supporting viruses {#sec-arbo-supporting}

Japanese encephalitis virus, a flavivirus, is kept going in a cycle between *Culex* mosquitoes and
animals: pigs and wading birds, in which it reaches levels in the blood high enough to infect
mosquitoes. Humans are a **dead-end host**, a host from which an organism is not passed on, because
too little virus reaches human blood, for too short a time, to infect a mosquito.
Japanese encephalitis is therefore a **zoonosis**, an infection transmitted from animals to humans
(see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain)). Its main harm is
**encephalitis**, inflammation of the brain.

| Virus | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Japanese encephalitis virus | Pigs and wading birds in rural Asia, carried by *Culex* mosquitoes that breed in rice fields and bite in the evening and at night | Humans are dead-end hosts, so the virus does not spread from person to person through mosquitoes; most infections are silent | In the few people who become ill, encephalitis that can be fatal or leave lasting damage to the brain; most cases are in children where the virus is common, because most adults there are immune. Prevented by vaccination |

### Later in the course {#sec-arbo-later}

| Virus | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| Dengue virus | Infectious diseases and general medicine (fever in Singapore, and fluid management in severe dengue); public health (vector control) |
| Zika virus | Obstetrics and neonatology (congenital infection); sexual health; public health (vector control) |
| Chikungunya virus | Rheumatology (joint pain that persists after the fever) |
| Japanese encephalitis virus | Neurology and paediatrics (encephalitis); travel medicine (vaccination) |
